sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities fell as a worldwide bond sell-off drove long-dated sovereign yields to multi-year highs. MSCI World slipped roughly **-1.2%** and MSCI Developed Markets a similar **-1.3%**, while MSCI Emerging Markets proved more resilient near **-0.4%**. The S&P 500 lost **1.4%** to **7,674** and the MAG7 mega-cap cohort underperformed, down around **-2.5%** as semiconductors led declines. Euro Stoxx 50 firmed **0.4%** to **6,447**, China's CSI 300 rose to **4,619** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng added **1.2%**, but Japan's Nikkei 225 tumbled **-3.9%**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities posted their first weekly loss since late July, snapping a three-week winning run. The S&P 500 fell **1.4%** to **7,674.37** and the Nasdaq Composite dropped **2.1%** to **26,180.45**, while the Dow logged back-to-back weekly declines of roughly **-1.8%** despite a Friday surge of **517.80** points, or **0.98%**, to **53,277.01** as small-caps rebounded.

The dominant catalyst was a global bond rout: the 30-year UST yield touched its highest since 2007 mid-week, with fiscal and deficit worries, heavy corporate supply and lingering inflation fears lifting the long end and compressing equity valuations, hitting rate-sensitive mega-cap tech hardest.

Semiconductors and the MAG7 led the weakness, and Walmart slid on cautious retail guidance, though an S&P Global PMI showing US business activity at its fastest pace in over four years cushioned sentiment. Investors positioned cautiously ahead of the Jackson Hole symposium and Chair Warsh's debut.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities were resilient, edging higher even as the sovereign bond sell-off intensified. The Euro Stoxx 50 rose about **0.4%** to **6,447**, Germany's DAX added roughly **0.3%** and the UK's FTSE 100 gained around **0.2%**, outperforming a weaker Wall Street.

The rates backdrop was the key theme: French 10-year yields hit their highest since 2008 and German Bund yields their highest since 2011, driven by fiscal-supply concerns and the global repricing of long-end debt, keeping duration-sensitive sectors under pressure.

Sector dispersion reflected the macro cross-currents, with energy names supported by firmer crude while higher discount rates weighed on growth and rate-sensitive plays. Relative to the US, contained regional inflation and steadier tech left European bourses comparatively insulated into the close.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets diverged sharply. Japanese equities led the declines as the Nikkei 225 tumbled about **-3.9%**, snapping a two-week advance, with semiconductor weakness spilling over from Wall Street and rising global yields sapping risk appetite; South Korea's KOSPI slid nearly **-6%** on the same chip-led selling.

Chinese equities bucked the trend. The mainland CSI 300 firmed to **4,619**, up **0.6%** on Friday, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose **1.2%**, buoyed by fresh fiscal support from Beijing, including consumer trade-in funding and a pledge of timely, incremental measures around a roughly **4%** of GDP deficit target.

The common thread was tension between a bond-driven risk-off tone in export- and tech-heavy North Asia and supportive Chinese policy signals, with the tech cycle, long-end yields and Jackson Hole guidance framing the outlook.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar stayed soft despite the bond rout, with the DXY hovering near **98.80**, close to its lowest since May, as the Treasury's plans to expand longer-dated debt buybacks and a cautious pre-Jackson Hole stance capped the greenback.

The euro held around **1.1670** and sterling traded in the low **1.3600s** ahead of a pivotal run of UK data that will test whether GBP's resilience extends beyond the risk-on backdrop. The yen lagged, with USD/JPY near **159.00** as wide rate differentials offset dollar softness.

Cross-asset volatility remained compressed, with the VIX near 2026 lows and the MOVE index easing, underpinning risk-sensitive and EM currencies even as record long-end sovereign yields kept the FX rate-differential narrative in focus.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Precious metals set the tone. Gold headed for a third consecutive weekly gain and a close near its 200-day moving average around **$4,514**, rallying even as nominal yields climbed, underscoring how fiscal and debt-sustainability concerns have become a primary driver of hard-asset demand.

Energy firmed on geopolitics: Brent rose to a near four-week high around **$95** after President Trump threatened Iran with economic warfare, before paring gains to about **$93.50**, with WTI near **$86.40**, reviving inflation worries just as long yields spiked.

Copper rallied despite London Metal Exchange inventories heading for their largest weekly build since 2020, supported by China's fresh fiscal stimulus. The cross-asset read was clear: fiscal, debt and geopolitical risks broadened the commodity rally and reinforced upward pressure on inflation breakevens.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign curves bear-steepened in a global sell-off. The 30-year UST yield closed near **5.27%** after touching its highest level since 2007 intra-week around **5.34%**, while the 10-year rose to roughly **4.73%**, driven by deficit worries, heavy corporate issuance and sticky inflation expectations.

The move was worldwide: French 10-year yields hit their highest since 2008 and German Bunds since 2011. Edward Jones expects the 10-year UST to trade between **4.5%** and **5.0%** over the remainder of the year, viewing higher yields as improving the strategic appeal of investment-grade bonds.

Strategists framed the rise constructively for income-focused investors even as it pressured equities. Credit tone stayed broadly firm, with IG spreads steady and HY resilient amid low volatility, though richer valuations and rate uncertainty argued for selectivity ahead of Jackson Hole.
